title: Gene expression
introduction: HL-only: learn how one DNA genome can give rise to distinct cell identities through transcription, RNA stability, chromatin changes and environmental responses.
learningPath: Evaluate epigenetic inheritance and environmental evidence
objectives: Differentiate promoter, enhancer and transcription-factor roles
Explain epigenetic changes without implying sequence mutation
Critically examine imprinting, twin comparisons and environmental evidence

sections.guidingQuestion: What links a protein-coding gene to a cellular trait?
sections.explanation:
A gene's DNA sequence can affect phenotype because the cell transcribes it into RNA and, for protein-coding genes, translates the mRNA into a polypeptide. The folded protein may serve as an enzyme, structural component, receptor or regulatory factor. Many phenotypic effects therefore emerge through a chain of molecular consequences.

Cells with similar DNA often differ in phenotype because they express different subsets and quantities of genes. Non-protein-coding functional RNAs also influence phenotype, so the DNA-to-protein path is common but not universal. Regulation acts at transcription, RNA stability, translation and later protein activity.

terms: Genes influence phenotype through expression: mechanism
Expression is not the DNA sequence itself: boundary or comparison
sections.workedExample: Pancreatic beta cells transcribe INS and produce insulin while most skin cells do not produce appreciable insulin.

misconceptions.misconception: Genes directly become proteins without any RNA intermediate.
misconceptions.correction: Most protein-coding genes act through transcription followed by translation and protein function.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which pair is directly involved in transcription initiation control?
sections.explanation:
Regulatory proteins recognize particular DNA sequences and change the probability that RNA polymerase begins transcription. Promoters define an initiation region; enhancers can be distant DNA elements that bind activators or other transcription factors. DNA looping or molecular interactions connect enhancer-bound proteins with promoter-associated machinery.

Cell identity and hormone signals influence which transcription factors are active. Activators or repressors can raise or lower transcription; a promoter is not an amino-acid sequence, and an enhancer does not need to be next to the gene to affect it.

sections.guidingQuestion: If mRNA is degraded faster while transcription stays constant, what generally happens to its abundance?
sections.explanation:
A newly made mRNA can be translated repeatedly while it persists. Nucleases eventually break RNA into smaller units, so differences in mRNA degradation rate influence how many protein molecules can be synthesized from one transcript. In human cells, some mRNAs last only minutes whereas others persist for hours or days.

Two cells could transcribe the same gene at similar rates but produce different protein amounts if one rapidly degrades its mRNA. It is therefore incorrect to infer protein synthesis rate from promoter activity alone; RNA abundance depends on both production and decay.

terms: mRNA lifetime controls protein production: mechanism

misconceptions.correction: mRNA degradation regulates how long transcripts remain available for translation.

sections.guidingQuestion: What makes epigenetic regulation distinct from sequence mutation?
sections.explanation:
During development, descendants of an embryo's cells acquire different patterns of gene expression as they differentiate. Transcription factors and chromatin states help stabilize these patterns so a neuron and a hepatocyte perform different functions despite broadly sharing the same inherited genome.

Epigenetic regulation changes gene activity or chromatin organization without changing the underlying DNA nucleotide sequence. A change in transcription does not by itself prove that a chromatin tag caused it; the explanation must connect regulatory mechanisms and cell identity.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which cellular dataset measures RNA molecules present at a given time?
sections.explanation:
A cell's genome is its total genetic DNA information; its transcriptome is the set and relative abundance of RNA transcripts present at a particular time; its proteome is its set of proteins present under those conditions. The same genome can support very different transcriptomes and proteomes.

An mRNA may change faster than its protein product; protein abundance also depends on translation, folding and degradation. Therefore transcript and protein measurements from the same cell need not agree directly. Not all genes are expressed in any one cell.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which statement about methylation is most accurate?
sections.explanation:
Methylation of cytosine in a promoter region is often associated with repression of the downstream gene, for example by preventing activator access or recruiting repressive proteins. Histone proteins in nucleosomes can also be chemically modified, altering how chromatin interacts with regulatory machinery.

Unlike the simplified notion that all methylation turns genes off, different histone methylation positions and patterns can be associated with gene activation or repression. For IB purposes, distinguish promoter DNA methylation from histone modification without memorizing individual histone residues.

sections.guidingQuestion: What may be inherited through mitosis without changing DNA sequence?
sections.explanation:
If an epigenetic pattern is maintained through mitosis, daughter cells can inherit similar gene-expression states without a nucleotide substitution. Some parent-of-origin marks can also influence offspring phenotypes, but germ-line and early embryonic reprogramming remove many marks.

Epigenetic inheritance across cell divisions is well established; widespread transmission of environmentally induced patterns across multiple human generations is far harder to demonstrate and should not be presented as routine. Molecular maintenance mechanisms and germ-line erasure constrain persistence.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which claim about air pollution and methylation is scientifically justified?
sections.explanation:
Environmental exposures such as air pollution are studied for associations with DNA methylation and altered gene-expression patterns. Pollution may affect oxidative stress, cell-signaling pathways and regulatory systems, but effects can differ by tissue, dose, timing and co-exposures.

A human epidemiological association between exposure and a methylation pattern must be interpreted with confounders, cell-type composition and measurement uncertainty. Controlled mechanistic experiments can strengthen a causal account; a single correlation does not prove that a methyl tag caused disease.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why might reciprocal mammalian hybrid crosses differ in phenotype?
sections.explanation:
During germ-cell and early embryonic development, many epigenetic marks are removed or re-established. Some imprinting-related marks and other protected patterns persist or are re-created in parent-specific ways, affecting how maternal and paternal contributions are expressed.

A male lion crossed with a female tiger produces a liger; reversing parental species produces a tigon. Their differences in growth are often discussed in relation to genomic imprinting and parent-of-origin gene expression, but body size is multifactorial and the exact causal explanation cannot be inferred from the phenotype alone.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the main research value of comparing monozygotic twins?
sections.explanation:
Monozygotic twins originate from one fertilized egg and generally begin with extremely similar DNA sequences. As they age, their environments, developmental histories and stochastic cellular events can differ, allowing researchers to study associations with gene expression and epigenetic marks.

Differences between identical twins are not automatically caused by environment alone: somatic mutations, cell mixtures, developmental randomness and technical effects can contribute. Well designed twin studies compare exposures, tissues and molecular outcomes while acknowledging shared early environments.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can lactose availability affect bacterial gene expression?
sections.explanation:
External hormone signals can bind cellular receptors and change activity of transcription factors. For example, glucocorticoid receptors can alter transcription of responsive genes. In bacteria, lactose metabolism provides another form of environmental regulation through a DNA-binding repressor.

When lactose is available, its derivative allolactose reduces lac-repressor binding to the operator, allowing increased expression of lactose-utilizing genes, especially when glucose is scarce. The mechanism is a regulatory response to the current environment, not a permanent change in bacterial DNA.

options.text: Transcription, translation and protein function
options.feedback: Correct. A gene's DNA sequence can affect phenotype because the cell transcribes it into RNA and, for protein-coding genes, translates the mRNA into a polypeptide.

questions.prompt: Explain the regulatory mechanism in genes influence phenotype through expression and evaluate the assertion "Genes directly become proteins without any RNA intermediate."
questions.answer: A gene's DNA sequence can affect phenotype because the cell transcribes it into RNA and, for protein-coding genes, translates the mRNA into a polypeptide. The folded protein may serve as an enzyme, structural component, receptor or regulatory factor. Many phenotypic effects therefore emerge through a chain of molecular consequences. Cells with similar DNA often differ in phenotype because they express different subsets and quantities of genes. Non-protein-coding functional RNAs also influence phenotype, so the DNA-to-protein path is common but not universal. Regulation acts at transcription, RNA stability, translation and later protein activity. Most protein-coding genes act through transcription followed by translation and protein function.

questions.prompt: Explain the regulatory mechanism in transcription factors read regulatory dna sequences and evaluate the assertion "Enhancers are proteins that move amino acids into a ribosome."
questions.answer: Regulatory proteins recognize particular DNA sequences and change the probability that RNA polymerase begins transcription. Promoters define an initiation region; enhancers can be distant DNA elements that bind activators or other transcription factors. DNA looping or molecular interactions connect enhancer-bound proteins with promoter-associated machinery. Cell identity and hormone signals influence which transcription factors are active. Activators or repressors can raise or lower transcription; a promoter is not an amino-acid sequence, and an enhancer does not need to be next to the gene to affect it. Enhancers are DNA regulatory regions that bind regulatory proteins.

questions.prompt: Explain the regulatory mechanism in mrna lifetime controls protein production and evaluate the assertion "Transcription rate alone determines the lifetime of every mature mRNA."
questions.answer: A newly made mRNA can be translated repeatedly while it persists. Nucleases eventually break RNA into smaller units, so differences in mRNA degradation rate influence how many protein molecules can be synthesized from one transcript. In human cells, some mRNAs last only minutes whereas others persist for hours or days. Two cells could transcribe the same gene at similar rates but produce different protein amounts if one rapidly degrades its mRNA. It is therefore incorrect to infer protein synthesis rate from promoter activity alone; RNA abundance depends on both production and decay. mRNA degradation regulates how long transcripts remain available for translation.

questions.answer: During development, descendants of an embryo's cells acquire different patterns of gene expression as they differentiate. questions.answer: A cell's genome is its total genetic DNA information; its transcriptome is the set and relative abundance of RNA transcripts present at a particular time; its proteome is its set of proteins present under those conditions. questions.answer: Methylation of cytosine in a promoter region is often associated with repression of the downstream gene, for example by preventing activator access or recruiting repressive proteins. Histone proteins in nucleosomes can also be chemically modified, altering how chromatin interacts with regulatory machinery. Unlike the simplified notion that all methylation turns genes off, different histone methylation positions and patterns can be associated with gene activation or repression. For IB purposes, distinguish promoter DNA methylation from histone modification without memorizing individual histone residues. summary: Regulatory DNA, transcription factors, RNA turnover and chromatin states determine gene-expression patterns; cells can differ in phenotype without different DNA sequences, and heritability of epigenetic changes is context-dependent.

The IB guide 2025 and Hodder 2023 D2.2 establish scope and depth; NIH and NCBI support regulatory distinctions.
